surveyDefinition.title: Home Coffee Machines — consumer survey (North America)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 5 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on brewing habits, machine type and usage, purchase drivers, and satisfaction with key machine attributes.

segments.name: Daily Ritualists
segments.description: Brew multiple cups every day, treat the machine as a central kitchen appliance, and value speed and consistency over experimentation. They are the heaviest users and often own a drip or pod machine.

segments.name: Convenience-Driven Users
segments.description: Brew one or two cups daily, primarily for a quick caffeine fix, and rely on pod or super-automatic machines. They value one-touch operation and minimal cleanup over brew quality.

segments.name: Specialty Users
segments.description: Actively pursue better coffee at home, own espresso or manual machines, and enjoy experimenting with beans and brew methods. They are willing to invest time and money for quality.

segments.name: Family Volume Brewers
segments.description: Brew for multiple household members, often in large batches, and need a machine that can keep up with volume. They prioritize capacity, counter space, and durability.

segments.name: Occasional Users
segments.description: Brew only a few times a week, often on weekends or for guests, and have low engagement with the category. They may own a basic machine and are not invested in upgrading.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Home Coffee Machines buyers in North America. It asks how people use Home Coffee Machines, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in North America who buy or use Home Coffee Machines for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Adults who own or intend to purchase a home coffee machine; Primary decision-makers for household appliance purchases; Coffee drinkers who prepare coffee at home at least several times per week. Excluded: Commercial coffee equipment buyers (cafés, restaurants, offices); Individuals who exclusively consume coffee outside the home; Non-coffee drinkers.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Household consumers buy home coffee machines for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the purchase themselves. While some businesses may buy espresso machines for offices, the core market is consumer households, making this a clear B2C segment.
respondentBehaviours: Regular coffee drinkers who brew at home daily or multiple times per week
Interested in specialty coffee and willing to invest in equipment for better quality
Research online before purchasing, comparing features and reviews
May be influenced by brand reputation and design aesthetics
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Brewing Context & Daily Ritual
sections.covers: Establishes who brews at home, how often, for whom, and what role coffee plays in their daily routine.

sections.label: Machine Acquisition & Purchase Drivers
sections.covers: Covers the journey from recognizing a need to choosing a machine, including triggers, research, channels, and what tipped the decision.

sections.label: Machine Requirements & Trade-offs
sections.covers: Identifies must-have features, quality cues, and the trade-offs buyers make between speed, noise, size, and brew quality.

sections.label: Satisfaction & Future Intent
sections.covers: Measures satisfaction with the current machine, pain points, and likelihood to recommend or replace.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's home brewing context — frequency, occasions, and household role — then moves through the acquisition journey, from trigger to channel to spend, before probing the specific product requirements and trade-offs that define their ideal machine. It closes with satisfaction, pain points, and future intent, allowing the data to separate the five segments on the basis of their brewing behaviour, purchase drivers, and priorities.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Home Coffee Machines in North America — who Adults who own or intend to purchase a home coffee machine; Primary decision-makers for household appliance purchases; Coffee drinkers who prepare coffee at home at least several times per week. The audience is defined as household consumers who are the primary users and purchasers of home coffee machines. This captures the core B2C market and excludes commercial buyers to keep the study focused on consumer behavior.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question cp8 (role of coffee in daily routine) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it explicitly asks respondents to categorize their relationship with coffee, cleanly separating ritual, caffeine fix, hobby, family, and occasional treat.
notes: Family volume brewers are identified by household size and capacity-related preferences; they may also brew multiple cups but not necessarily for themselves.
Occasional users are identified by low frequency, guest-oriented brewing, and low spend.
Specialty enthusiasts are identified by manual/espresso machines, high spend, and desire for variety and quality.
Convenience-driven users are identified by pod/super-auto machines, quick caffeine fix, and acceptance of worse coffee for convenience.
Daily ritualists are identified by high daily volume, morning ritual, and sensitivity to speed.
6 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=250 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's home brewing context — frequency, occasions, and household role — then moves through the acquisition journey, from trigger to channel to spend, before probing the specific product requirements and trade-offs that define their ideal machine. It closes with satisfaction, pain points, and future intent, allowing the data to separate the five segments on the basis of their brewing behaviour, purchase drivers, and priorities.
storyline_notes: Dropped the generic 'category relationship' beat in favor of a direct 'home brewing status' confirmation, since the target audience is already qualified as home brewers.
Added a 'brew types used' beat in the requirements section to capture the versatility dimension that separates specialty enthusiasts from convenience users.
Included 'design and footprint' as a format beat because counter space is a top pain point in this category and a key differentiator for compact-space dwellers.
The acquisition section includes a 'purchase cycle' beat to capture replacement timing, which is essential for a durable appliance category.

The satisfaction section explicitly includes 'pain points' as a separate beat to capture the known top frustrations (noise, heat-up, drip tray) and to separate segments on their tolerance for these trade-offs.

The segments are cut on usage behaviour and jobs-to-be-done, not on price sensitivity alone, because the same price point can serve very different usage needs — a family volume brewer and a specialty enthusiast may both spend $500 but want
metadata.classification_reason: Household consumers buy home coffee machines for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide on the purchase themselves. While some businesses may buy espresso machines for offices, the core market is consumer households, making this a clear B2C segment.
